In the SQLite large-batch branch, values is grown with fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) once per ID. This copies the entire accumulated string on every iteration, making building the IN list O(n^2); with the newly tested batch size of 32767 IDs the final string is hundreds of kilobytes and is re-copied tens of thousands of times. Use strings.Builder (or strconv.AppendInt into a []byte) to build the list in linear time.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Several dual-writer metrics are recorded against the wrong storage or label

When Storage.Create fails, Create calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recording a storage failure, and Update does the same at its storage-error path. DeleteCollection records the asynchronous legacy result with recordStorageDuration, while Delete's success path passes the resource name where other calls pass options.Kind as the kind label. This corrupts the mode-3 dashboards/error attribution and, for Delete, introduces a high-cardinality metric label containing object names.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment ('Delete's success path passes the resource name where other calls pass options.Kind as the kind label'), alongside a few other related metric recording issues.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the cancellable request context

Create derives the legacy goroutine's context from the incoming request context, and the same pattern is used by Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. The API server can cancel that context as soon as Create returns the unified-storage response, which happens immediately after spawning the goroutine, so the legacy write will often run with an already-cancelled context and fail. This defeats the stated safety purpose of mode 3. The legacy context needs to be detached from request cancellation, for example with context.WithoutCancel plus its own timeout, while preserving needed values.

Unordered legacy goroutines can resurrect or lose objects

Every Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection launches an independent legacy goroutine with no per-resource ordering or queue. Rapid operations on the same object can therefore reach legacy storage out of order: a delete can run before the preceding create and leave a resurrected object, or an update can run before its create and be lost. The previous synchronous implementation preserved request order, so legacy storage can now silently diverge from unified storage.

Create shares the same object between the response and legacy goroutine

Create passes the original obj pointer to the asynchronous Legacy.Create while returning the unified-storage result to the caller. The storage implementation may have mutated obj, and the caller/API server may concurrently serialize or mutate the returned object while the goroutine reads the same underlying object, creating a data race. The legacy call can also observe storage-assigned fields such as resourceVersion that a legacy create does not expect. Legacy needs its own deep copy made before the goroutine is started.

Update recomputes the updated object separately for legacy storage

Update now passes the original objInfo to Legacy.Update after Storage.Update has already consumed it. Each storage will invoke UpdatedObject against its own old object, so transformations, defaults, timestamps, or other computed fields can differ between unified and legacy storage, and a stateful UpdatedObject implementation may fail or behave differently on the second call. The removed updateWrapper existed to compute the object once and give both stores the identical result; that guarantee needs to be restored for the legacy write.

Delete no longer cleans up legacy objects when unified delete reports NotFound

Delete now returns immediately for any Storage.Delete error. The previous implementation specifically tolerated NotFound and still attempted the legacy delete. An object that exists only in legacy storage, or whose unified copy was already removed, will now remain in legacy storage and can reappear if traffic is rolled back to a legacy-reading mode. NotFound from unified storage should still trigger the legacy deletion attempt.

Asynchronous legacy failures are silently swallowed

The legacy goroutines in Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection capture the legacy error only to update a duration metric and never log it. The previous synchronous implementation logged legacy write failures. Operators therefore get no object identity or error context when legacy storage starts diverging, making the safety copy unreliable and difficult to diagnose or reconcile.

Mode 3 tests never synchronize with or verify the async legacy writes

The new Create and Update tests register legacy mock expectations but return immediately after asserting only the unified-storage result; Delete and DeleteCollection do not meaningfully verify a legacy call at all. Nothing waits for the goroutines, calls AssertExpectations, or uses.Eventually, so a legacy write that never happens can still pass, while a goroutine running after the test finishes can produce racy or unexpected mock calls. The async behavior that defines mode 3 is therefore untested.

New mode 3 integration cases immediately assert legacy visibility despite async writes

The added file and unified-storage mode 3 cases reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates, updates, and deletes through the Kubernetes API and then immediately checks the legacy playlist API for the same state. Mode 3 performs legacy writes in fire-and-forget goroutines with no completion signal, so those legacy assertions race the asynchronous writes and will be flaky even if they usually win the race in local runs.

runShardSplitQuery() now interpolates every target with datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters), and splitQueriesByStreamShard() then passes each shard sub-request to runSplitQuery(), which interpolates the same targets again with the same scopedVars and filters. The updated shard test confirms this: one original query now causes applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times. applyTemplateVariables is not just placeholder substitution for dashboard variables; it also applies request.filters/ad-hoc filters and variable formatting/escaping. Re-applying it can duplicate ad-hoc filters in the LogQL expression and can re-expand $-sequences introduced by the first replacement, corrupting the query or changing the stream selector, in addition to repeating the work for every shard group. If all targets interpolate to empty, runSplitQuery builds zero grouped requests and runSplitGroupedQueries() dereferences requests.filter(...)[0].partition after Math.max(...[]) , throwing a TypeError instead of completing with no data. The same regression is introduced in runShardSplitQuery(), which changed from interpolate-then-filter to filter-then-interpolate. Targets need to be filtered again after interpolation.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Validation performs a database write, so match statistics are counted repeatedly

EmailValidator calls BlockedEmail.should_block? during validation, and should_block? increments and saves match_count/last_match_at. Validation is not a one-time commit event: UsersController#create calls user.valid? and then user.save (which validates again), so one blocked signup attempt increments the counter at least twice, and any other code that merely calls valid?/save on a user with a changed email also records a 'match' even if the user is never persisted. Move the accounting out of the predicate/validator or make it happen once per create attempt; a validator query should be side-effect free.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same underlying issue: the predicate method `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (or `should_block_email?`) performs database writes (updating match statistics) as a side effect of a read/validation check, which shouldn't have side effects.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email matching is case-sensitive and can be bypassed

BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up the exact string with `where(email: email)`, and BlockedEmail neither downcases nor strips the address before saving or lookup. A blocked address such as bad@spam.com can therefore be resubmitted as Bad@Spam.com or with surrounding whitespace and miss the block, while the case-insensitive portions of Discourse treat those as the same email. The unique database/model check is likewise case-sensitive, so differently-cased duplicates of a blocked address can coexist. Normalize with the same email downcasing used elsewhere on both record creation and lookup (and ideally a case-insensitive uniqueness guarantee).
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same vulnerability: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a case-sensitive email lookup, which allows bypassing email blocks by altering the case of the email address.

false_positives.candidate:
match_count increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write

`record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save` reads a value, increments it in memory, and writes it back. Two concurrent registration attempts matching the same blocked email can read the same count and both save count+1, losing an increment, and the full-record save can also overwrite concurrent changes to fields such as action_type. Use an atomic database increment (e.g. update_counters/increment_counter or a single UPDATE ... SET match_count = match_count + 1) for the statistics update.

The new email validator never checks that the value is an email address

EmailValidator.validate_each only applies the whitelist/blacklist domain settings and the BlockedEmail check; it contains no format check. Since User now relies on `validates :email, email: true` (app/models/user.rb:47) as its email validator, a direct API request with a malformed value such as 'not-an-email' passes server-side validation as long as it is present and unique, creating an account whose activation/welcome mail can never be delivered. Add a format validation (using the project's existing email format rules) before the domain/blocked checks.

The validator spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and calls validate_each directly on a fabricated user, while blocked_email_spec tests BlockedEmail in isolation. Nothing exercises the full path that a User with a real blocked email fails to save through `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, so a broken validator registration, autoload problem, or email_changed? condition would let blocked signups through while all new specs still pass. Add a User-level example (and a whitelist/blacklist example for the logic moved out of User) that saves/validates against a real BlockedEmail record without stubbing.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
align-items mixin passes incompatible values to legacy alignment properties

The mixin passes $alignment unchanged to -webkit-box-align and -ms-flex-align, but those legacy properties accept start/end rather than flex-start/flex-end, so a caller using the standard align-items value flex-start or flex-end will get invalid legacy declarations and lose alignment in the prefixed browsers this mixin targets. It also emits -ms-align-items, which is not the IE10 property. The mixin should translate flex-start/flex-end to start/end for the legacy properties. Current callers use center and baseline, which happen to be spelled the same in both syntaxes.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly notes that the mixin 'emits -ms-align-items, which is not the IE10 property' alongside its observation about value mapping for `-ms-flex-align` and `-webkit-box-align`. Thus, it successfully identifies the exact issue mentioned in the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order mixin mistranslates values for legacy box ordinal groups

The mixin copies $val directly to -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group, but legacy ordinal groups are 1-based (initial value 1 and values below 1 are invalid) while flex order is 0-based (initial value 0). Consequently order(0) emits an invalid legacy declaration and the legacy translation does not faithfully represent the standard value; the legacy properties should use $val + 1.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` and `-moz-box-ordinal-group` are 1-based and do not accept 0 as a valid value, so passing `$val` (specifically when `$val` is 0) directly causes invalid legacy CSS and layout issues.

false_positives.candidate:
Flex conversion breaks right-aligned small-action button

Making .small-action a flex container makes its direct children flex items, and floats do not apply to flex items. The button rule at lines 306-310 still relies on float: right, with no margin-left: auto, justify-content, or other flex positioning to replace it. A small-action delete button will therefore sit immediately after .small-action-desc instead of at the right edge of the post row.

Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name predicate is missing the question mark

ActiveModelSerializers decides whether to emit an attribute by calling `include_<attribute>?`, as used by every other predicate in this serializer (e.g. include_email?, include_stats?). The new method is named `include_website_name` without `?`, so it is never invoked: `website_name` is serialized for every user, with a nil value when the user has no website, instead of being omitted as intended.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the primary bug described in the golden comment: the `include_website_name` method is missing the required `?` suffix for ActiveModelSerializers to conditionally include the attribute. Although the golden comment also mentions a secondary issue regarding string mutation (`<<`), the core issue is clearly matched.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses the untrusted-user field restrictions

`website_name` is added to the public attributes but not to the `untrusted_attributes` list (lines 105-111), which hides fields such as `website`, `location` and `bio_cooked` from anonymous viewers of TL0 users via scope.restrict_user_fields?. Because website_name is derived directly from the hidden website, an anonymous visitor can still learn a TL0/spam account's website host and, in the same-domain case, its full path, defeating the restriction that hides `website` itself.

website_name discards the query string and fragment

The display text is built as `website_host + URI(website).path`, so for a website such as `http://example.com/blog?author=alice` or `http://example.com/#about` the serialized name becomes just `example.com/blog` or `example.com/`. The PR's goal is to show the complete URL when it points at the instance's domain, but the shown text silently loses the query/fragment that distinguishes the target (the href still contains it, so text and link disagree).

Same-domain detection only works for subdomains of equal depth

The elsif branch treats two hosts as the same base domain only when they have the same number of labels and everything after the first label matches (e.g. www.example.com vs forum.example.com). A website at blog.example.com (3 labels) viewed on an instance at www.forum.example.com (4 labels) falls through to the final branch, fails the ends_with? parent check, and loses its path even though both are under example.com; conversely the drop-first-label heuristic equates unrelated sites under a shared suffix such as alice.blogspot.com vs an instance-related bob.blogspot.com. The result is inconsistent with the stated same-domain rule.

No spec covers the sibling-subdomain branch or restricted visibility of website_name

The new specs cover only an unrelated domain, an exact host match, and a parent-domain website. They do not exercise the elsif sibling-subdomain branch in website_name (www.example.com vs forum.example.com, or the negative case where the remaining labels differ), nor the TL0-user-seen-as-anonymous context at the top of the file, so neither a regression in that branch nor website_name leaking for restricted users would be caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Embed URL is interpolated unescaped into raw HTML

TopicEmbed.import appends an imported-from footer by interpolating the supplied URL directly into an href attribute and link text. The URL is checked only for an http/https prefix, so a URL containing a single quote or markup can close the attribute or element and inject additional HTML. Because the resulting post uses raw_html cooking, that injected markup is stored and rendered without the normal cooking sanitization.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the XSS vulnerability caused by unescaped URL interpolation into HTML within the `TopicEmbed.import` method, which is one of the two core issues described in the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feed polling crashes on items without content

poll_feed unconditionally calls i.content.scrub for every feed item. RSS items commonly provide only a description or summary and can therefore have nil content, raising NoMethodError. Because there is no per-item rescue, one such item aborts the entire hourly poll, prevents all remaining items from being imported, and will recur on every run until the feed changes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: calling `i.content.scrub` when `i.content` is nil (because RSS feeds often only provide a description/summary) will cause a crash/NoMethodError.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Referer is embedded unescaped in a JavaScript string

The embed layout interpolates request.referer directly inside a single-quoted JavaScript string passed to parent.postMessage. A referer containing an apostrophe or crafted path can terminate the string and alter the script executed on the Discourse-origin embed page. The target origin should be derived and serialized safely on the server, for example by extracting the referer's origin and emitting it with proper JavaScript/JSON escaping.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same vulnerability: the unescaped interpolation of `request.referer` into JavaScript, which leads to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) / arbitrary script execution.

false_positives.candidate:
Imported feed HTML is stored and rendered without sanitization

TopicEmbed.import creates posts with cook_method raw_html for content supplied by Jobs::PollFeed, and Post#cook returns that raw content verbatim as cooked HTML. The PollFeed path does not pass the content through Readability or any HTML sanitizer, so script elements, event-handler attributes, javascript: URLs, and other active markup from an RSS/Atom item are persisted and later rendered to forum readers. This is a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability if any imported feed item contains malicious or compromised content.

Unknown embeds enqueue an unbounded retrieval job on every request

EmbedController#best enqueues Jobs::RetrieveTopic whenever no TopicEmbed exists, with no controller-side throttling or deduplication. The 60-second throttle is only checked after a job is dequeued, and the loading page automatically reloads, while non-browser clients can spoof the Referer check trivially. Repeated or malicious requests for a URL that can never be retrieved can therefore flood the Sidekiq queue indefinitely.

Remote import fetches arbitrary redirected URLs without timeouts or size limits

TopicEmbed.import_remote calls open(url).read with no timeout, response-size limit, or validation of the final URI after redirects. TopicRetriever validates only the initial embed_url host, so a page on the embeddable host can redirect the server-side request to another host, including internal services, and a slow or very large response can tie up a background worker or exhaust memory. A bounded HTTP fetch that revalidates redirect targets is needed.

Disqus import now depends on live remote pages and aborts on fetch failures

The Disqus importer replaces local topic creation with TopicEmbed.import_remote for each thread link. If a link is missing, stale, offline, or returns an HTTP error, open() raises and aborts the whole Thor import, leaving later threads unprocessed; if import_remote returns no post, that thread's Disqus comments are silently skipped. Previously the topic could be created from the export itself, so this change risks losing exported comments solely because the original site is unavailable.

Embed controller spec expects synchronous retrieval the controller no longer performs

The spec expects TopicRetriever.new and retrieve to be called when no embed exists, but EmbedController#best never references TopicRetriever; it enqueues Jobs::RetrieveTopic instead. Mocha will report the unmet TopicRetriever expectation, so this test fails and provides no valid coverage of the actual enqueue behavior. The spec should expect the retrieve_topic job enqueue with the user id and embed_url.

Protocol-relative URLs are incorrectly rewritten to the source host

absolutize_urls treats every href or src beginning with '/' as a path on the source host. Protocol-relative URLs such as //cdn.example.com/image.jpg therefore become http://source-host/cdn.example.com/image.jpg instead of retaining the CDN host, breaking external links and images in imported content; the same faulty transformation is applied to img src attributes below. Protocol-relative and ordinary relative URLs need distinct handling.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Second downsize definition overrides the existing width/height API

Ruby does not support method overloading by arity. This new three-argument downsize definition replaces the width/height version defined immediately above it at lines 145-147. Existing callers using downsize(from, to, width, height) will now treat width as a complete dimensions string and height as opts, producing wrong geometry or a TypeError, while callers passing width, height, and opts will raise ArgumentError. The old signature must be retained compatibly or every existing caller updated.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: the `downsize` method is defined twice, and because Ruby does not support method overloading, the second definition (taking a single dimensions string) overrides the first (taking separate width and height arguments), breaking existing callers.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hard-coded 10 MB client limit ignores per-type site settings

validateUploadedFile receives a type and previously used the corresponding max_image_size_kb or max_attachment_size_kb setting. Replacing that lookup with a fixed 10 MB value means attachments larger than 10 MB are rejected even when the site allows them, while non-image attachments above a lower configured attachment limit pass the client check, are not downsized by the server, and then fail only after being uploaded. The same hard-coded value is repeated for the 413 error at line 246. The image pre-downsizing allowance should not replace attachment validation or disregard configured limits.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same problem: replacing the dynamic per-type site setting lookup with a hardcoded 10MB limit causes client-side validation to diverge from configured settings (including in the 413 error handler).

false_positives.candidate:
In-place downsizing ignores conversion failure and can destroy the upload

OptimizedImage.downsize returns false when conversion or optimization fails, but this call ignores the result and uses the same tempfile path as both input and output. A failed or partial ImageMagick/ImageOptim operation can therefore truncate or corrupt the only copy of the uploaded file, after which the loop retries the failed operation up to five times and line 72 proceeds with whatever remains. Downsizing should write to a separate file, check the result, and only replace the original after success.

No server-side size limit is enforced before expensive image conversion

The 10 MB limits added elsewhere are only in client-side JavaScript and in the URL-download branch. A direct multipart request can bypass JavaScript and submit a much larger image, causing this code to run as many as five full ImageMagick and ImageOptim passes before Upload.create_for performs its normal size validation. An authenticated user can consequently trigger very large CPU, memory, and disk consumption, including with a highly compressed image that expands greatly when decoded. The controller should enforce the intended maximum input size server-side before invoking downsizing.

Downsizing is applied unsafely to SVG and animated image originals

The condition accepts every filename considered an image and sends it through convert with the first-frame selector. This bypasses the SVG special case elsewhere in OptimizedImage, where SVG files are copied rather than converted, so an oversized vector can be rasterized, invalidated, or changed in format. Likewise, when animated thumbnails are disabled, an animated GIF original is reduced to its first frame rather than merely having a static thumbnail. SVG handling and preservation of animation for the stored original need separate treatment.

No tests cover the new downsizing behavior

The pull request adds a percentage-based OptimizedImage.downsize form, a five-attempt controller loop, changed client limits, and changed download limits, but includes no spec or JavaScript test changes. There is therefore no coverage proving percentage geometry works, that the loop terminates at the configured byte limit, that conversion failure preserves or rejects the upload safely, or that animated and vector images retain their expected format.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe crashes when the user has no TopicUser row

TopicUser.find_by can return nil, for example when a mentioned or invited user, or a different logged-in user opening a forwarded email link, has never created a topic_users row for this topic. The next line calls tu.notification_level on nil, raising NoMethodError and returning a 500 instead of creating or updating the notification level.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: `tu` (obtained via `TopicUser.find_by`) can be `nil` when a `TopicUser` record does not exist, and subsequently calling methods on `tu` will cause a crash/NoMethodError.

false_positives.candidate:
State-changing unsubscribe is performed by an unauthenticated-token GET request

The unsubscribe action mutates TopicUser.notification_level on a plain GET and the email link contains no signed token tied to the recipient. Any page, image, mail scanner, or link prefetcher that loads the URL in a logged-in browser will change that session user's notification level without a confirmation or CSRF token, and a forwarded link acts on whoever is logged in rather than the intended recipient.

Unsubscribe downgrade is not idempotent, so refreshing changes the level again

The action downgrades exactly one step on every GET: watching/tracking (levels 3/2) becomes regular (1), and a subsequent reload of the same unsubscribe URL then turns regular into muted (0). The final state therefore depends on how many times the email link is opened, prefetched, or refreshed, rather than always ending at the intended unsubscribed state.

Template name does not match the topicUnsubscribe route

The route added in app-route-map.js.es6 is the top-level route topicUnsubscribe, whose route, controller, and view files are all named topic-unsubscribe, so Ember looks for a topic-unsubscribe template. This file is registered as topic/unsubscribe, which corresponds to a nested topic.unsubscribe route that is never defined, so the unsubscribe outlet will not render this template and the page can be blank or raise a missing-template error.

unsubscribe_link now requires unsubscribe_url for every add_unsubscribe_link email

config/locales/server.en.yml adds %{unsubscribe_url} to the shared unsubscribe_link translation, and both body and html_part interpolate it from template_args, which has no default for unsubscribe_url. Email::MessageBuilder previously allowed add_unsubscribe_link: true by itself (the existing spec did exactly that before being edited here); any such caller or plugin mailer that does not also pass unsubscribe_url will now raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument and fail to send.

Direct save! bypasses TopicUser.change bookkeeping

set_notifications and other notification-level changes go through TopicUser.change, which sets notifications_changed_at and notifications_reason_id and publishes a MessageBus notification_level_change. Assigning tu.notification_level and calling save! skips all of that, so open clients keep showing the old watching/tracking state and the change is recorded without the usual reason or timestamp.

No tests cover the new unsubscribe endpoint

The PR adds a state-changing TopicsController#unsubscribe action but the only spec change adds an unsubscribe_url argument to an existing MessageBuilder example without asserting the URL reaches the body. There is no controller spec exercising level transitions for watching/tracking/regular/muted users, the missing-TopicUser case, slug redirects, or unauthenticated access, so the main regressions in this feature would not be caught.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp is always formatted in en-US regardless of user locale

true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same problem: a date/timestamp is being formatted with a hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of utilizing the user's locale from the `useLocale` hook.

false_positives.candidate:
Successful cache deletion does not refresh the connected-calendars query

The deleteCache mutation only shows a toast and calls the optional onSuccess callback, unlike the disconnect mutation below it which invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars on settle. In SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper the internal suspense query that supplies cacheUpdatedAt is therefore not refetched (onChanged is an optional external callback and may be undefined), so after a successful deletion the dropdown keeps showing the old timestamp and 'Delete cached data' action until a manual reload.

A credential whose cache expired long ago is therefore reported to the UI as having a current cache with a 'Last updated' timestamp and a delete action, even though that cache is never used.

Callers that pass relation data allowed by this signature will fail Prisma validation at runtime; the signature should use the update-many mutation input type (and the sole caller in CalendarService.ts passes {} relying on implicit @updatedAt behaviour rather than an explicit updatedAt value).

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

resourceStore.findByType(server, "Clients") also returns the synthetic all-Clients resource created by AdminPermissionsSchema.init, whose name is the literal string "Clients". When the caller has an all-clients grant, the returned set contains "Clients" instead of (or in addition to) real client UUIDs, and when only an all-clients grant exists no actual client ids are returned at all. Callers expecting a set of client ids to filter client listings will match nothing for the all-clients case. The synthetic resource must be excluded and an all-clients grant expanded to real clients (or handled by the caller).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying bug: getClientsWithPermission queries typed Clients resources and returns the synthetic "Clients" resource name rather than actual client IDs. Although the candidate describes filtering failures instead of the golden comment's null client lookup, the faulty resource selection and ID mismatch are the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NullPointerException when the all-Clients resource does not exist

In hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when no client-specific resource exists the code loads the all-Clients resource via getResourceTypeResource and immediately calls policyStore.findByResource(server, resource) without a null check (the String overload of hasPermission does check for null). getResourceTypeResource returns null whenever the Clients resource was never provisioned - e.g. realms whose admin-permissions client was created before the Clients type existed, since AdminPermissionsSchema.init returns early when that client already exists - so every canView/canManage/canConfigure check for such a realm throws instead of returning false, breaking admin client operations with a 500.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same issue: getResourceTypeResource can return null in ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, and passing that null resource to findByResource without a defensive check can cause a NullPointerException.

false_positives.candidate:
canView(ClientModel) bypasses a client-specific negative permission

canView(ClientModel) returns true immediately when canView() is true, and V2 canView() only evaluates the all-Clients resource for VIEW. If an administrator is granted VIEW on all clients but explicitly denied VIEW on one sensitive client through a negative policy on that client's resource, requireView(sensitiveClient) still passes. The client-specific denial is never evaluated, unlike canManage/canConfigure which evaluate the specific client resource, so the denied client remains directly viewable.

Role-mapping checks do not imply manage or the manage-clients admin role

canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only evaluate their exact FGAP scope and never fall back to canManage(client). An administrator with the MANAGE_CLIENTS realm role, or with a V2 MANAGE permission for the client (which canManage/canConfigure treat as the higher privilege), is therefore denied mapping that client's roles, composites, and client-scope roles. This is inconsistent with the manage > configure > view transitivity implemented elsewhere in this class and with the Users V2 behaviour where manage implies map-roles.

Listener still calls V2-unsupported methods when both FGAP features are enabled

The listener is now guarded only by Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1), but AdminPermissions.management()/evaluator() prefer MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever the V2 feature is also enabled. With both features on, deleting a client fires ClientRemovedEvent, passes the new guard, and calls MgmtPermissionsV2.clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false), which in ClientPermissionsV2 unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException. The guard needs to also exclude the V2 case (or management() must not return the V2 implementation here), otherwise client deletion fails or logs an exception and the V1 cleanup is not performed.

getResourceName has no Clients branch

getResourceName only special-cases the Users resource type (returning "All users" or the username) and falls through to resource.getDisplayName() for everything else. Client resources created by getOrCreateResource are named by the client UUID and have no display name set, so authorization representations for the new Clients permissions will show a null/blank or raw-UUID name instead of "All clients" or the client's clientId. Add the analogous Clients branch resolving the client via session.clients().

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
VIEW permission is treated as MANAGE for global group operations

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() returns true when the caller has either VIEW or MANAGE on the all-Groups resource. This no-arg check is used by GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() via requireManage(), so an admin granted only view on all groups can create top-level groups. canManage() should require MANAGE only, as canManage(GroupModel) correctly does.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(): accepting VIEW permission alongside MANAGE incorrectly grants management/write access to view-only users. The candidate additionally describes a concrete affected operation.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses authorization resource IDs instead of group IDs

In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(), groupResource.getId() is the internal authorization-resource UUID, while the group's ID is stored as the resource name (see AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource/resolveGroup, and hasPermission() which looks resources up by name). Passing getId() to hasPermission() therefore fails the findByName lookup and falls back to the all-Groups resource, and the set returned contains authorization UUIDs rather than group IDs. Callers such as UsersResource.getUsersCount() and searchForUser() pass this set to user queries as group IDs, so counts/searches for members of a group with view-members/manage-members permission return wrong (typically empty) results.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same resource-ID versus group-ID mismatch in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission: getId() is passed to a name-based permission lookup and returned for group filtering, causing fallback to the all-groups resource and incorrect user filtering/counts.

false_positives.candidate:
Existing FGAP V2 realms never get the new Groups resource or scopes

AdminPermissionsSchema.init() returns immediately when the realm already has an admin-permissions client. Realms that enabled admin permissions before this PR therefore never receive the new 'Groups' all-resource or the group-only scopes (manage-members, view-members, manage-membership) that init() would create from the schema. Creating a group permission in such a realm will fail when getOrCreateResource() cannot find those scopes, and getResourceTypeResource() for Groups will return null during evaluation. A migration/backfill for existing resource servers is needed.

getResourceName does not translate group resources to group names

getResourceName() special-cases the Users resource type to return the user's username instead of the resource name (which is the user's ID), but has no equivalent branch for the new Groups resource type. Group resources are also named by their group ID, so policy/permission representations for group resources will fall through to resource.getDisplayName() and expose the group UUID rather than a human-readable group name.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns an unrelated JVM-default KeyStore provider

The CryptoProvider contract states that getBouncyCastleProvider returns the BouncyCastle (or BCFIPS) provider, but this implementation returns the provider associated with KeyStore.getDefaultType(), typically SUN/SunPKCS12 and configurable through JVM security settings. Callers that use the returned provider by name or expect BouncyCastle-only services such as BCFKS or AES/CBC/PKCS7Padding can therefore fail or silently use a different provider depending on JVM configuration. If no BouncyCastle provider is available, the method should fail clearly or return null as other non-BC providers do rather than masquerading as BouncyCastle.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JVM-default KeyStore provider rather than the BouncyCastle provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

Adding abstract int order() to the public CryptoProvider interface is source- and binary-incompatible for implementations outside this repository. Existing compiled implementations will throw AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration invokes order() through its comparator, and existing source implementations will no longer compile. A default method, for example returning 0, would preserve compatibility while allowing the built-in providers to declare their higher precedence.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the backward-compatibility break caused by adding an abstract order() method to CryptoProvider, requiring existing implementations to implement it.

false_positives.candidate:
Equal-order providers are silently and nondeterministically selected instead of failing fast

DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, and WildFlyElytronProvider all return order() 200. This change sorts providers by order and silently uses the first one, retaining ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order for ties and only logging the ignored providers at debug level. If the default and FIPS providers, or Elytron and default providers, accidentally coexist on the classpath, the selected provider is therefore classpath-dependent; in particular a non-FIPS provider can silently be selected in an environment expecting FIPS cryptography. Previously detection failed fast when multiple providers were present. A tie for the highest order should still fail, or the mutually exclusive server providers should have distinct deterministic priorities.

ECDSA tests use one default EC key and only verify self-consistent round-tripping

The test creates a single EC key pair without specifying a curve, so on the usual SunEC provider it is a P-256 key even for the ES384 and ES512 cases, while the conversion is told to use 48- or 66-byte R/S components and merely zero-pads the P-256 values. It also only asserts concat -> DER -> concat round-tripping with the same implementation under test and never compares the DER result with the original Signature.sign() output or verifies it with Signature.verify(). A standards-incorrect but self-consistent encoder/decoder pair, or incorrect curve-length handling for real P-384/P-521 signatures, can therefore pass; each algorithm should use a key on its corresponding curve and validate against the JCA signature.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined before asserting that no exceptions occurred

The background reader thread is started without keeping a reference, and after deletedAll is set the test immediately asserts that caughtExceptions is empty. The reader may still be in the middle of a groups request at that point and may add the very server-error exception this regression test is meant to catch only after the assertion has passed, so the test can pass spuriously. The unjoined thread can also leak into subsequent tests and keep calling the admin API; if a deletion throws, deletedAll is never set and the loop can run indefinitely. Store the thread, stop it in a finally block, and join it before asserting on caughtExceptions.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: the test sets deletedAll and asserts before waiting for the reader thread to finish, allowing exceptions to be recorded after the assertion. The candidate's additional concerns do not change this core match.

false_positives.candidate:
Other subgroup-stream methods still dereference a possibly deleted delegate

The fix recognizes that modelSupplier.get() can return null when the cached group is deleted concurrently, but the three paginated/search getSubGroupsStream overloads at lines 256, 262, and 268 still call modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...) without a null check. If deletion occurs after the GroupAdapter is obtained but before one of these methods delegates to the database, the same concurrent-deletion scenario therefore still produces a NullPointerException and a server error instead of being handled consistently with getSubGroupsCount().

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Call to non-existent no-argument isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation

UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method added in UsernamePasswordForm is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user). UsernameForm, UsernamePasswordForm, and their superclasses define no no-argument overload, so this code does not compile and the services module cannot be built.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() without the required UserModel argument. The candidate additionally explains that the missing argument causes a compilation failure.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Passkey conditional UI is now disabled for initial login where no user is set yet

isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel) requires user != null, and it gates fillContextForm() in authenticate() (line 115) and challenge(error, field) (line 137). On an initial UsernamePasswordForm login the context user is still null, including for discoverable-passkey login, so the WebAuthn challenge, RP ID and conditional-UI attributes are never put on the login form. This reverses the previous user==null behaviour instead of extending it to re-authentication, regressing first-login passkey authentication and removing passkeys from the form re-rendered after an initial-login error.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same regression: requiring a non-null user prevents authenticate() from calling fillContextForm() on the initial login page, disabling conditional passkey UI and ID-less passkey authentication. The candidate's additional error re-render concern does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Comma-joined shard metric tag corrupts per-shard metrics for shared processes

shard_tag is built by joining multiple shard IDs with commas and then used as a single metric tag value. This is the common case when one flusher process handles several shards, including the CLI default of one process. In StatsD-style tag encoding, commas separate tags, so a value such as '0,1,2' is parsed as shard:0 plus stray tags rather than one shard dimension, making the produce and segment-size metrics unusable for per-shard analysis. The wait_produce timer at line 199 also inconsistently names the tag 'shards' instead of 'shard'. Emit metrics per shard or use a sanitized single-value grouping tag consistently.
true_positives.reasoning: Although the candidate primarily discusses comma-joined tag values, it also explicitly identifies the golden issue: wait_produce uses 'shards' while produce and segment-size metrics use 'shard', and recommends consistent tagging.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hung flusher processes are never killed before replacement

In production, processes are created with multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, producing SpawnProcess objects. SpawnProcess is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process (the default-context process class on Linux), so isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is false and process.kill() is never called. _create_process_for_shards then starts a replacement for the same shards while the hung original remains alive; both can call flush_segments and produce for the same Redis shards, causing duplicate segment production and leaked processes. The check should use multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or exclude threading.Thread instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same incorrect isinstance check: spawn-context processes are SpawnProcess objects, not subclasses of multiprocessing.Process on POSIX, so hung flusher processes are not killed. The candidate adds consequences and potential fixes without changing the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() can return without terminating all flusher processes

join() waits for processes sequentially against a shared deadline. If the deadline expires while waiting for an early process, the loop breaks and never calls terminate() on the remaining processes. The terminate() call that is reached is also guarded by isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process), which is false for SpawnProcess objects created through the spawn context. A process hung in flushing or producing can therefore survive join() and continue running alongside a new flusher after rebalance, risking duplicate flushes. Daemon status does not help because the parent consumer process remains alive across rebalances.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same deadline-triggered loop break that skips terminate() calls for remaining flusher processes, leaving them running. Its additional concern about the process type guard does not change this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Invalid flusher process counts are not validated

max_processes is accepted without requiring a positive value. An explicit 0 is treated by 'max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)' as unset and unexpectedly spawns one process per shard, while a negative value makes num_processes negative, creates an empty process_to_shards_map, and then fails with an opaque KeyError when shards are assigned. Since --flusher-processes accepts any integer in src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py, operators can trigger either excessive process creation or a consumer startup crash instead of a clear configuration error. Validate the value at the CLI and/or SpanFlusher boundary.

New multiprocess test never exercises spawning or actual multi-shard flushing

test_flusher_processes_limit passes produce_to_pipe, which forces SpanFlusher to use threading.Thread instead of the production spawn-process path, and it only asserts process counts and shard-map totals without submitting or flushing any spans. Consequently the tests do not cover spawn pickling of per-shard SpansBuffer objects, run_with_initialized_sentry argument handling, per-process Kafka production, shared-process flushing for multiple shards, or process kill/restart behavior. A regression in the production multiprocess path could pass while the consumer duplicates or loses flushed segments.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Table widget feature flag renders a hardcoded empty table

When the organization has the use-table-widget-visualization feature, tableResultComponent ignores the actual tableResults entry and renders TableWidgetVisualization with columns=[] and tableData containing empty data and empty meta. Every dashboard table for such an organization will therefore appear blank regardless of the query results, loading state, fields, or title. The real result data must be converted and passed to the new visualization instead of the hardcoded empty placeholder.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: when the feature flag is enabled, TableWidgetVisualization receives hardcoded empty data rather than actual query results, causing the table to render empty.

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Browser report validation does not require exactly one of age or timestamp

The serializer makes both age and timestamp optional and only rejects them when the other field is truthy via self.initial_data.get(...). A report with neither field is accepted even though it conforms to neither supported Reporting API format, and a report with age=0 or timestamp=0 together with the other field also passes because 0 is falsy. This allows malformed reports to be counted as valid. Enforce presence of exactly one field using key presence rather than truthiness.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same truthiness-based validation bug: .get(...) treats zero-valued timestamps as absent, allowing age=0 and timestamp together to bypass mutual-exclusion validation. It also recommends checking key presence, matching the golden fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Assemble analytics are recorded before the feature-flag check

The endpoint records the preprod_artifact.api.assemble analytics event before checking organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble and before validating the request body. Requests from organizations without the feature, which return 404, and malformed requests, which return 400, are therefore counted as artifact assembly events and pollute downstream analytics. Move analytics.record after the feature and validation checks, ideally only for requests that actually proceed toward assembly.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same issue: analytics are recorded before the feature flag check, so requests returning 404 because the feature is disabled are incorrectly logged. Its additional concern about validation failures does not change the match.

false_positives.candidate:
Error and breadcrumb timestamps are compared in different units

fetch_error_details stores the error event timestamp as a Unix timestamp in seconds, while recording-segment events from rrweb carry timestamps in milliseconds. gen_request_data directly compares error_events[error_idx]['timestamp'] with event['timestamp'], so virtually every error will compare as earlier than the first breadcrumb and all errors will be emitted at the start instead of in chronological order. Normalize both timestamps to the same unit before sorting and interleaving.

Hidden span attributes are only hidden while searching

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES is checked only inside the filter that runs when searchQuery is non-empty. When the search box is empty, sortedAndFilteredAttributes returns the sorted attributes unchanged, so is_segment, project_id, and received are still displayed by default and disappear only after the user starts typing a search. Apply the hidden-attribute exclusion before or independently of the search-text filter.

Issue titles are inserted unescaped into a Markdown link

MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE interpolates the issue title directly into link text as [**{title}**]({url}). Issue titles are derived from error data and can contain closing brackets or Markdown link syntax, so a title containing a sequence such as ](https://example.invalid) can break out of the intended link, corrupt the PR comment formatting, or substitute a misleading destination. Escape or strip Markdown link delimiters from the truncated title before formatting the template.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset branch crashes because Django querysets reject negative slicing

When enable_advanced_features is true and a client supplies a cursor with a negative offset, this branch executes list(queryset[start_offset:stop]) with start_offset < 0 (and stop may also be <= 0). The comment claims the Django ORM handles negative slicing automatically, but Django QuerySet slicing explicitly raises AssertionError: "Negative indexing is not supported." A privileged audit-log user can craft e.g. a cursor with offset -1 and turn the request into a 500 instead of getting the claimed reverse-pagination behavior.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator uses negative slice offsets on Django querysets, which reject negative slicing and raise an AssertionError.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unconditional dereference of organization_context.member can crash non-optimized requests

enable_advanced is computed for every request as request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access, even when optimized_pagination is not requested. RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is optional (None when the caller has no membership record for the organization), and because of the unconditional evaluation before the branch, such a request raises AttributeError and returns 500 instead of serving the normal DateTimePaginator path. The member check should be guarded (e.g. member is not None) and ideally only evaluated when use_optimized is true.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unguarded access to organization_context.member.has_global_access when member is None, causing an AttributeError. The candidate emphasizes non-optimized requests rather than API-key/org-token requests with optimized pagination, but the underlying null-dereference bug is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator is incompatible with datetime ordering used by audit logs

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key() applies math.floor/math.ceil directly to getattr(item, self.key), and value_from_cursor() returns cursor.value unchanged. The audit-log endpoint uses this paginator with order_by="-datetime", so the key is a datetime: math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError when build_cursor() computes next/prev cursors, causing a 500 on the first optimized page. Even if that did not crash, returning the raw millisecond cursor value instead of converting it to a datetime like DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor() would make build_queryset() compare a datetime column against an integer. The optimized audit-log path is therefore unusable.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil to a datetime when the audit-log endpoint uses order_by="-datetime", causing a TypeError. The additional cursor-conversion concern does not change this direct match.

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator change still allows negative offsets for previous-page cursors on every endpoint

The new line clamps the offset only when cursor.is_prev is false: start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset. Cursor values are client-controlled (parsed from the cursor query parameter), so any user of any BasePaginator/DateTimePaginator/Paginator endpoint can supply a negative offset with is_prev=1 and still reach queryset[negative:stop], which Django rejects with AssertionError. This ungated change to the shared paginator does not fix the negative-index crash it appears to address and leaves a trivially triggerable 500 across all endpoints using these paginators, not just the admin-gated audit-log path.

New OptimizedCursorPaginator and endpoint branch have no test coverage

The PR adds a new paginator class, modifies shared BasePaginator slicing, changes Cursor documentation to endorse negative offsets, and adds a new query-param/permission-gated branch in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint, but includes no tests. A single test exercising OptimizedCursorPaginator with the endpoint's actual -datetime ordering, plus tests for negative, zero, and previous-page cursors, would have caught the datetime TypeError and Django negative-slicing AssertionError described above before merge.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key are no longer serialized or deduplicated

BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for its whole duration; now it only locks when inserting the finished index and never re-checks whether the same NamespacedResource was built concurrently. Two concurrent Search/handleEvent calls through getOrCreateIndex can both miss GetIndex and build the same key: for file-backed indexes both use the same directory path, so one can fail on the already-open index, and for memory indexes one finished index is overwritten in the cache and leaked without Close. Add per-key/single-flight building or a double-checked cache lookup under an appropriate lock.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: narrowing cacheMu locking from the entire BuildIndex operation to only the final cache insertion allows concurrent calls to build the same expensive index for the same key. The candidate adds consequences and remedies without changing the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu

bleveBackend.TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without acquiring cacheMu, while BuildIndex now writes b.cache at the end of a potentially long concurrent build. Concurrent map iteration and map write can cause Go's fatal 'concurrent map iteration and map write' panic. This can be reached when searchSupport.init starts its watch goroutine before logging TotalDocs and a watch/search request lazily builds another index. TotalDocs should hold cacheMu.RLock for the iteration.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization while BuildIndex can write to it concurrently after the watcher starts, potentially causing a concurrent map iteration/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
searchSupport.init has unsynchronized writes from errgroup workers

In searchSupport.init, every errgroup worker executes totalBatchesIndexed++ and assigns to the shared outer err variable (line 190). These concurrent unsynchronized writes are a data race, can lose counter increments for the span attribute, and make the shared err value racy/redundant because errgroup already collects worker return values. Use an atomic counter and a local error variable inside each worker.

NewResourceServer performs blocking index builds with an uncancellable background context

NewResourceServer now synchronously calls s.Init(ctx), but ctx is derived internally from context.Background and is only cancelled by server.Stop, which cannot be called until the constructor returns. A slow or hung GetResourceStats/ListIterator index build therefore blocks construction indefinitely with no caller-supplied startup context or timeout, and a search-index failure now prevents creation of the whole resource server including non-search operations. Pass a caller context/timeout into construction or otherwise make eager initialization cancellable.

Constructor does not clean up partial initialization on Init failure

When s.Init fails in NewResourceServer, the function returns nil, err without calling s.cancel or lifecycle Stop. Init may already have started side effects, notably searchSupport.init's background-context watch goroutine or a partially started watcher, but the discarded server gives the caller no handle to stop them. This leaks goroutines/pollers that continue consuming storage events after construction has failed; clean up the server context and started components on the error path.

Postgres storage-server integration coverage is disabled instead of fixed

The change adds an unconditional postgres skip to TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer just as the PR changes storage-server startup to eagerly initialize unified storage. That removes CI coverage for the eager Init/SQL path on one supported database backend, so a postgres-specific startup regression would not be caught. Fix the underlying postgres failure or keep the skip tied to a tracked, narrowly scoped condition.

false_positives.candidate:
Queues are unbounded, so the strategy provides no backpressure

FixedQueuePool creates every work queue with queue.Queue() and no maxsize, and submit() therefore never blocks or raises MessageRejected. The Arroyo processor can keep polling Kafka and enqueueing messages faster than workers process them, causing unbounded memory growth in both the queues and OffsetTracker's offset sets and potentially an OOM. This also contradicts the strategy docstring's claim of natural backpressure when queues fill up.

Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed

OrderedQueueWorker.run catches any exception from result_processor, logs it, and then unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset in the finally block. The commit loop can consequently commit offsets for messages whose processing failed, so those Kafka messages will not be redelivered or sent to a DLQ. This contradicts the strategy's stated guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing.

Shutdown flag causes workers to abandon queued items

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown=True before shutting down the queues, while OrderedQueueWorker.run checks that flag at the top of every loop iteration. A worker blocked in get() may process at most one queued item after shutdown begins and then exit, leaving the rest of its queue unprocessed despite queue.shutdown(immediate=False) being intended to drain it. Graceful shutdown therefore strands accepted work; those offsets remain uncompleted and the messages must be reprocessed after restart.

Commit loop is stopped before queued work is drained

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before calling queue_pool.shutdown(). Any offsets completed by workers while the pool is draining afterwards have no commit thread left to commit them, so successfully processed messages are not checkpointed on graceful close and will be delivered and processed again after restart.

Closing a strategy destroys the shared pool reused after rebalance

ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool and passes that same object to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy it creates, but this strategy's close() shuts the shared pool down. Arroyo closes and joins the old strategy when partitions are revoked and then creates a new strategy from the same factory for the new assignment, so the new strategy reuses queues that are already shut down and workers that have exited. Subsequent puts raise queue.ShutDown, which SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches and then marks the offset complete, allowing unprocessed messages to be committed and permanently lost after a routine rebalance.
