The redirect-following loop previously allowed depth 10000 and documented that deeper segment trees might not be joined correctly. Reducing it to 1000 without a corresponding product limit means traces with redirect chains deeper than 1000 are split into multiple segments, producing incomplete segments and incorrect root/segment assignment. Deep-tree tests only exercise a handful of spans and do not cover this regression.

Insert-time eviction silently truncates segments using a hardcoded limit

The script always ZPOPMIN-evicts down to 1000 spans, ignoring SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (whose Python default is 1001 and which callers can configure), and records no metric or log for discarded spans. Legitimate large segments are now silently flushed as incomplete data rather than being handled by the previous explicit oversized-segment path. Because eviction removes the lowest end_timestamp_precise scores and the separate has-root flag is not recomputed, an evicted segment/root span can also leave the has-root state inconsistent with the remaining payloads, while evicted span IDs remain in the redirect hash until expiry.

Flush-time max_segment_spans protection is removed and the setting becomes dead

_load_segment_data no longer enforces self.max_segment_spans or emits the segment_span_count_exceeded metric/log; after this change the constructor setting has no remaining effect in the flush path. Any segment that bypasses the Lua cap, including data produced by another writer or a future merge change, can now be loaded and emitted without the previous span-count bound, risking oversized Kafka messages and memory pressure. If insert-time eviction is intended to replace this check, the obsolete setting and its contract should be removed consistently rather than left silently ignored.

No test covers the new eviction or sorted-set merge behavior

The updated buffer tests only add the required end_timestamp_precise field to existing small cases; every scenario uses at most five spans. There is no test that inserts more than the eviction limit, verifies which spans are retained, checks behavior when the segment/root span would be evicted, exercises duplicate payloads across merged sorted sets, or verifies redirect chains near the reduced depth limit. The central behavioral change of the PR is therefore untested.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset

_get_event_stats executes against its scoped_dataset argument, but is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects is called with the closure variable dataset. The dashboard-split factory calls _get_event_stats with discover or another split_dataset while dataset may be metrics_performance/metrics_enhanced_performance, so error split queries are incorrectly judged ineligible and never upsampled; conversely a transaction-like scoped query can inherit eligibility from the outer dataset. Pass scoped_dataset to the eligibility check.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the eligibility check using the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset. Both also cite the same consequence: in the dashboard split path the query runs on discover while the outer dataset is metrics, so upsampling is skipped.

false_positives.candidate:
upsampled_count drops events whose sample_weight is NULL instead of counting them once

The aggregate is sum(sample_weight) with no coalesce/ifNull fallback. Allowlisted projects will contain events without client error sampling (historical events, unsampled/default events, events from SDKs that do not set the context), and any row with NULL sample_weight contributes 0 rather than 1, so enabling upsampling can collapse those buckets to undercounted or zero counts. The new tests only store events with client_sample_rate=0.1 and never cover this case. Use a fallback such as sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1)).

Error-focus detection ignores the actual query being executed

_is_error_focused_query re-reads request.GET['query'] and only matches the exact substring 'event.type:error'. _get_event_stats receives an explicit query argument that callers modify, e.g. the dashboard-split path builds '({query}) AND !event.type:transaction' and other derived queries, but the helper cannot see those strings, so eligibility is decided from a different query than the one sent to Snuba. It also misses equivalent formatting/casing variations of the executed query. Thread the query argument through is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects/_should_apply_sample_weight_transform instead of reading the request.

Internal upsampled_count function is exposed for direct user queries

The new SnQLFunction 'upsampled_count' does not set private=True, unlike internal-only functions around it. Because the function converter also resolves user-supplied yAxis values, any caller can request yAxis=upsampled_count() directly for any project or event type, bypassing the allowlist and error-only gating in error_upsampling.py and obtaining weighted counts (or meaningless zeroes where sample_weight is absent). Mark it private so only the server-side column transformation can introduce it.

Accidental nested-repository gitlink added to the repository root

This adds 'sentry-repo' as a subproject/gitlink pointing at the base commit, with no .gitmodules entry or purpose described in the PR. It is unrelated to upsampling and will pollute the tree, confuse submodule/checkout tooling, and should be removed before merge.

Cache invalidation helper is dead code, so allowlist changes have no invalidation path

invalidate_upsampling_cache is introduced with a docstring saying it should be called when the allowlist configuration changes, but nothing in the PR (or the option-setting machinery) calls it. Eligibility is cached for 60 seconds under a key derived only from organization and project ids, so removing a project from the allowlist keeps returning upsampled counts, and adding one keeps returning raw counts, until TTL expiry, with no way to force consistency. Either wire invalidation into the allowlist change path or remove the helper and document that TTL expiry is the only mechanism.

Integration tests miss the errors dataset, topEvents, and unsampled-event cases

The new Snuba tests only exercise the default/discover timeseries path with fully sampled events. They do not cover dataset=errors (a branch _should_apply_sample_weight_transform explicitly enables), the separate topEvents transformation branch in _get_event_stats, or an allowlisted project containing events without error_sampling context. Those are exactly the paths where an unregistered function, a missed column transformation, or NULL sample_weight handling would silently fail or return wrong counts, so add cases for them.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test does not actually prove the denial short-circuit

The test comment says it allows access through permCache to prove that path is not checked, but it stores map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. With that value, the cached-permission check would also deny, and the fallback fake store returns no permissions, so the test would still pass if the denial-cache early return were removed. The cached permission should be true and the test should preferably assert that the permission store is not consulted, so it genuinely verifies that a denial entry takes precedence.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point out the same mismatch: the test comment says the cached permission allows access, but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so the check would deny anyway. The candidate adds that this means the test doesn't really prove the denial short-circuit, but the underlying issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key does not uniquely identify an authorization check

userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, raw user UID, action, resource name, and parent with underscores, and its caller does not include the identity type. Anonymous and render subjects both use UID 0, so an anonymous denial can incorrectly deny the render service for the same action, resource, and folder even though the render service is granted read access. The ambiguous underscore encoding also makes distinct pairs such as name='a_b', parent='c' and name='a', parent='b_c' produce the same key. These collisions can incorrectly deny unrelated checks until the denial entry expires.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly describes the ambiguous underscore concatenation in userPermDenialCacheKey causing collisions (a_b/c vs a/b_c) and wrong denial cache hits, which is the golden issue. It also raises an extra point about identity type, but the core issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Negative cached checks re-query permissions for every distinct resource

When cached permissions do not allow a request, Check unconditionally calls getIdentityPermissions, and the user/anonymous permission paths no longer consult permCache before querying the permission store. The new denial cache only suppresses repeats for the exact namespace/user/action/name/parent combination. Consequently, checking N distinct resources that a user legitimately cannot access causes N permission-store queries, even though the first query has just refreshed that user's permissions for the action. This removes the permission cache's protection for negative authorization checks and can create substantial database load when many resources are checked or filtered.

Denial cache blocks permissions granted after an initial denial

Check returns immediately from permDenialCache before re-querying permissions, while line 154 populates that cache after any fresh denial for the shortCacheTTL period. If a dashboard or folder is created, a creator permission is added, or an administrator grants access after an initial denied check, subsequent identical checks continue to return false without consulting the database until the denial expires. An intervening check during creation can therefore poison access to the newly created resource and defeat the PR's intended fresh-permission re-query for up to the denial TTL.

Refreshed permission check still uses stale folder tree and then caches the denial

After a cached check fails, Check re-runs checkPermission with refreshed permissions, but inherited-permission evaluation still uses buildFolderTree's cached folder tree and does not refresh or invalidate it. For a dashboard in a newly created folder whose access is inherited from an ancestor folder, the ancestor lookup can miss because the new folder is absent from the cached tree; the resulting false result is then stored in permDenialCache at line 154. This both prevents the permission re-query from fixing newly created nested resources in this case and can extend the incorrect denial beyond the folder cache's own expiry.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:

The new check directly indexes integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]. Integrations created before sender metadata was recorded, or created through paths where no sender was stored, do not have this key. If such an ACTIVE integration remains after its OrganizationIntegration is removed and someone attempts to install it again, this line raises KeyError/TypeError and returns a 500 instead of either proceeding safely or showing the intended invalid-installation page. The metadata should be read defensively and a missing sender handled explicitly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: integration.metadata['sender']['login'] is indexed directly, which raises a KeyError when the sender metadata is missing.

false_positives.candidate:
Sender validation is bypassed when the Integration row does not exist yet

GitHubInstallation only compares github_authenticated_user with the installer when an Integration row already exists. If Integration.objects.get raises DoesNotExist it immediately calls pipeline.next_step(), which proceeds to create and link the integration. The Integration row is normally created by GitHub's asynchronous installation webhook, and GitHub provides no ordering guarantee between that webhook and the browser redirect/OAuth pipeline. A user whose GitHub login differs from the installer can therefore claim the installation if they reach this step before the webhook is processed, or if the webhook is delayed or missed, defeating the validation added by this PR.

GitHub token-exchange and user-info failures are not converted to the installation error page

safe_urlopen at line 423 is called outside the try block, and get_user_info at line 434 is also unguarded. Network failures, GitHub HTTP errors, or an invalid/unusable access token can therefore raise out of OAuthLoginView.dispatch and produce a 500. This contradicts the PR's stated behavior that failures to obtain a valid access token or verify the GitHub user should show the invalid-installation error page.

OAuthLoginView uses GitHubIdentityProvider.get_oauth_client_id/get_oauth_client_secret, which are the github-login.* credentials for GitHub SSO, not the github-app.client-id/github-app.client-secret credentials used to configure the GitHub App integration. Deployments that configured only the GitHub App, as previously sufficient for installing this integration, will now redirect to GitHub with an empty or invalid client_id and cannot complete installation at all. The flow should use the GitHub App's OAuth credentials or otherwise not make GitHub login configuration a new prerequisite.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation-not-found path

The test replaces the GitHub installation endpoint with a 404, but its second setup request supplies a state value that does not match the pipeline signature, so OAuthLoginView returns the generic invalid-installation page before build_integration can call the installation endpoint. The 404 stub is therefore never meaningfully exercised and the assertion would pass even if the installation-not-found handling regressed; the test needs a valid OAuth state/code exchange before asserting the 404 behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.

false_positives.candidate:
getForLogin loses the delegate's deterministic ordering

The cached path collects identity-provider IDs into a Set and then builds a HashSet<IdentityProviderModel> (lines 244-254) before returning identityProviders.stream(). This discards the ordering of idpDelegate.getForLogin(), which concatenates realm-level providers before organization providers and otherwise follows the storage query order. Callers of getForLogin that do not explicitly sort (the login bean does, but other broker/manager callers may not) will now observe arbitrary, potentially call-varying ordering instead of the previous deterministic order.

getLoginPredicate() now evaluates Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC)) for every identity provider whose organizationId is non-null, without checking getConfig() for null. IdentityProviderModel config is settable and can be null for models built from representations or by custom code. Previously the predicate only called isEnabled/isLinkOnly/isHideOnLogin and could not fail this way. In the new cache code this predicate is invoked from create/update/remove in InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider before the delegate operation runs, so a null-config organization-linked IdP would fail creation/update/removal with an NPE instead of being processed.

Login cache aggregates an unbounded entry per organization under three keys

cacheKeyForLogin creates only one cache key per FetchMode, while organizationId is stored as the searchKey inside a single IdentityProviderListQuery. Every distinct organizationId first seen for a mode therefore goes through the miss branch (lines 233-241), invalidates the whole shared object, and re-adds a new query copied from the previous one. In realms with many organizations this creates one retained ID set per organization ever queried under REALM_ONLY/ORG_ONLY/ALL, makes adding each new organization copy all previously cached variants, and means the REALM_ONLY cache also accumulates spurious per-organization entries even though that mode ignores organizationId. This is unbounded cache growth and invalidation churn proportional to the number of organizations.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
SQL feature gate contains inverted dead logic and always returns false

enableSqlExpressions computes enabled as !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions), then returns false both when enabled is true and when it is false. The feature-flag value therefore has no effect, the variable name and negation misrepresent the security intent, and the function unnecessarily dereferences h.features even though it can never return true; a reader constructed without feature toggles would panic on a SQL query instead of cleanly rejecting it. Replace this with an unconditional return false (with a comment explaining SQL expressions are disabled) or remove the helper and reject directly at the call site.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say the enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic and always returns false, which disables SQL expressions regardless of the feature flag. The candidate identifies the same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand entry point is not explicitly disabled

The explicit SQL-expression rejection is added only to ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery in pkg/expr/reader.go, while UnmarshalSQLCommand here still accepts a SQL expression and forwards it to NewSQLCommand. It is currently blocked only incidentally because the stubbed sql.TablesList/RunCommands returns 'not implemented', producing a misleading 'error reading SQL command' BadRequest; there is no explicit disabled check or feature/feature-toggle awareness on this path. If the in-memory DB implementation is later restored, this entry point silently becomes functional again without passing through the reader.go gate. Reject SQL commands explicitly on this unmarshalling path as defense-in-depth.

No regression tests cover the disabled SQL-expression behavior

This security change makes RunCommands and QueryFramesInto always return 'not implemented', makes pkg/expr/sql.TablesList always fail, makes NewSQLCommand always fail, and makes the reader reject QueryTypeSQL, but the PR changes no _test.go files. Existing tests that expect table parsing or SQL execution to succeed will now fail or need skipping, and there is no new regression test proving a SQL expression is rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled (the CVE scenario) via both the reader path and UnmarshalSQLCommand. Add/update tests asserting the disabled behavior so a future refactor of enableSqlExpressions or the DB stub cannot silently re-enable the vulnerable path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock

The fast path checks the cache under RLock at lines 41-46, but after a goroutine waits for the exclusive lock at line 48 it unconditionally reloads the manifest and overwrites entryPointAssetsCache at line 69. Consequently, if several non-Dev requests arrive concurrently on a cold cache, every one of them performs the file read instead of all but the first reusing the newly populated cache. Add a second check after acquiring Lock (only for cfg.Env != setting.Dev, so Dev reload behavior is preserved) to return the populated cache.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same flaw: the double-checked locking is incomplete because the cache is not re-checked after the write lock is acquired.

false_positives.candidate:
No concurrent regression test for the race fix

The change adds synchronization to GetWebAssets but no test exercises concurrent calls, so CI running with -race has no coverage that would catch a regression of the reported data race on entryPointAssetsCache. Add a test that resets the global cache, serves a temporary assets-manifest.json, and calls GetWebAssets from many goroutines simultaneously (cold-cache non-Dev path, and ideally the Dev reload path), asserting all callers succeed with the same assets.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Successful cleanup batches are logged at Error level with the full ID list

The new batch loops in CleanAnnotations (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (lines 576, 579) call r.log.Error unconditionally, including on success where the logged err value is nil. Every batch of a routine cleanup will therefore emit error-level log lines, which pollutes logs, can trigger error alerting, and prints the entire ids slice (potentially tens of thousands of IDs for large batch sizes) on every iteration. These should be removed or downgraded to Debug and should not dump the full ID list.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: Error log level is used for routine or debug information, which pollutes error logs. Both suggest downgrading to Debug. The candidate adds a point about dumping full ID lists, but its core concern is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Global cleanup ticker shortened from 10 minutes to 1 minute without justification

The ticker that drives CleanUpService.clean() is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This does not only affect annotation cleanup: the same clean() run executes temporary-file, snapshot, dashboard-version, image, user-invite, short-URL, and query-history cleanup. All of those jobs will now run ten times as often, increasing database and filesystem load on every Grafana instance, and the PR description gives no reason for this unrelated change. It looks like a leftover local-testing change and should be reverted or justified separately.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the cleanup ticker being changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute and the resulting increase in database load from more frequent cleanup runs. They describe the same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Placeholder-limit workaround only handles SQLite, so large batches still fail on PostgreSQL/MySQL

deleteByIDs special-cases only SQLite when AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize exceeds 999; for all other databases it builds one DELETE ... WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...) with len(ids) bound parameters. PostgreSQL's extended protocol allows at most 65535 parameters per statement (MySQL has similar placeholder/packet limits), so a configured batch size above that now makes every cleanup batch fail, whereas the previous subquery-based DELETE had no parameter-count limit regardless of batch size. The workaround should be based on the actual number of IDs and the target dialect's limit, chunk the DELETE, or inline IDs for large batches on all dialects.

Split SELECT/DELETE for MaxCount can delete annotations that are back within the retention count

For MaxCount cleanup, IDs are selected with ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT batch OFFSET MaxCount and then deleted by ID in a separate, non-transactional statement. If one of the newest MaxCount annotations is deleted (e.g. via the annotation Delete API) between the SELECT and the DELETE, a fetched ID moves into the set that should now be retained, but it is still deleted, leaving fewer than MaxCount annotations. The old single-statement DELETE evaluated the offset atomically. The PR description only acknowledges under-deletion on concurrent inserts; this concurrent-delete path causes over-deletion beyond the configured retention policy.

SQLite inline ID list is built with repeated fmt.Sprintf string concatenation

In the SQLite large-batch branch, values is grown with fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) once per ID. This copies the entire accumulated string on every iteration, making building the IN list O(n^2); with the newly tested batch size of 32767 IDs the final string is hundreds of kilobytes and is re-copied tens of thousands of times. Use strings.Builder (or strconv.AppendInt into a []byte) to build the list in linear time.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Several dual-writer metrics are recorded against the wrong storage or label

When Storage.Create fails, Create calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recording a storage failure, and Update does the same at its storage-error path. DeleteCollection records the asynchronous legacy result with recordStorageDuration, while Delete's success path passes the resource name where other calls pass options.Kind as the kind label. This corrupts the mode-3 dashboards/error attribution and, for Delete, introduces a high-cardinality metric label containing object names.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says Delete's success path passes the resource name where other calls pass options.Kind as the kind label. That is the same inconsistency the golden comment describes. The candidate also raises other metric issues, but this one matches.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the cancellable request context

Create derives the legacy goroutine's context from the incoming request context, and the same pattern is used by Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. The API server can cancel that context as soon as Create returns the unified-storage response, which happens immediately after spawning the goroutine, so the legacy write will often run with an already-cancelled context and fail. This defeats the stated safety purpose of mode 3. The legacy context needs to be detached from request cancellation, for example with context.WithoutCancel plus its own timeout, while preserving needed values.

Unordered legacy goroutines can resurrect or lose objects

Every Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection launches an independent legacy goroutine with no per-resource ordering or queue. Rapid operations on the same object can therefore reach legacy storage out of order: a delete can run before the preceding create and leave a resurrected object, or an update can run before its create and be lost. The previous synchronous implementation preserved request order, so legacy storage can now silently diverge from unified storage.

Create shares the same object between the response and legacy goroutine

Create passes the original obj pointer to the asynchronous Legacy.Create while returning the unified-storage result to the caller. The storage implementation may have mutated obj, and the caller/API server may concurrently serialize or mutate the returned object while the goroutine reads the same underlying object, creating a data race. The legacy call can also observe storage-assigned fields such as resourceVersion that a legacy create does not expect. Legacy needs its own deep copy made before the goroutine is started.

Update recomputes the updated object separately for legacy storage

Update now passes the original objInfo to Legacy.Update after Storage.Update has already consumed it. Each storage will invoke UpdatedObject against its own old object, so transformations, defaults, timestamps, or other computed fields can differ between unified and legacy storage, and a stateful UpdatedObject implementation may fail or behave differently on the second call. The removed updateWrapper existed to compute the object once and give both stores the identical result; that guarantee needs to be restored for the legacy write.

Delete no longer cleans up legacy objects when unified delete reports NotFound

Delete now returns immediately for any Storage.Delete error. The previous implementation specifically tolerated NotFound and still attempted the legacy delete. An object that exists only in legacy storage, or whose unified copy was already removed, will now remain in legacy storage and can reappear if traffic is rolled back to a legacy-reading mode. NotFound from unified storage should still trigger the legacy deletion attempt.

Asynchronous legacy failures are silently swallowed

The legacy goroutines in Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection capture the legacy error only to update a duration metric and never log it. The previous synchronous implementation logged legacy write failures. Operators therefore get no object identity or error context when legacy storage starts diverging, making the safety copy unreliable and difficult to diagnose or reconcile.

Mode 3 tests never synchronize with or verify the async legacy writes

The new Create and Update tests register legacy mock expectations but return immediately after asserting only the unified-storage result; Delete and DeleteCollection do not meaningfully verify a legacy call at all. Nothing waits for the goroutines, calls AssertExpectations, or uses.Eventually, so a legacy write that never happens can still pass, while a goroutine running after the test finishes can produce racy or unexpected mock calls. The async behavior that defines mode 3 is therefore untested.

New mode 3 integration cases immediately assert legacy visibility despite async writes

The added file and unified-storage mode 3 cases reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates, updates, and deletes through the Kubernetes API and then immediately checks the legacy playlist API for the same state. Mode 3 performs legacy writes in fire-and-forget goroutines with no completion signal, so those legacy assertions race the asynchronous writes and will be flaky even if they usually win the race in local runs.

useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities/useGrafanaPromRuleAbility convert skipToken to undefined, and useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities treats an undefined rule as supported: loading is false, isProvisioned/isPluginProvided are false, so MaybeSupported becomes AlwaysSupported. useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously computed isFederated with isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) for CombinedRule callers and used it to block Update/Delete/Pause for federated groups. It now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hard-codes isFederated=false. Federated Mimir/cloud rule groups can consequently be presented as editable, removable, and pausable even though they should remain immutable in the UI.

Rule detail link drops the returnTo parameter

The previous GrafanaRuleListItem built its view link with createReturnTo() so navigating to the rule detail could return to the current list context. The new component links only to `/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view` with no returnTo. Users opening a rule from the filtered or grouped list lose that explicit return destination and may not be taken back to the same list state.

runShardSplitQuery() now interpolates every target with datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters), and splitQueriesByStreamShard() then passes each shard sub-request to runSplitQuery(), which interpolates the same targets again with the same scopedVars and filters. The updated shard test confirms this: one original query now causes applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times. applyTemplateVariables is not just placeholder substitution for dashboard variables; it also applies request.filters/ad-hoc filters and variable formatting/escaping. Re-applying it can duplicate ad-hoc filters in the LogQL expression and can re-expand $-sequences introduced by the first replacement, corrupting the query or changing the stream selector, in addition to repeating the work for every shard group. Interpolation should happen once, e.g. runSplitQuery needs a way for the shard path to indicate targets are already interpolated.

Queries are now interpolated on line 299 before partition() calls querySupportsSplitting() on line 300. querySupportsSplitting() deliberately refuses to split queries containing $__range, $__range_s, or $__range_ms because those macros must be evaluated against the final request range (see the comment at lines 285-287). If applyTemplateVariables resolves those range macros from the request scoped vars, the token is gone by the time the guard runs, so a query that must not be split is split into daily chunks while keeping the full-range macro value baked into each chunk. That changes rate/count_over_time semantics at chunk boundaries and can return incorrect data. The range-variable check needs to run on the pre-interpolation expression, or range macros must be excluded from this early interpolation.

The empty-expression filter runs before interpolation (lines 296-299), so a target whose whole expression is a variable, e.g. expr='$var', passes the filter and only becomes '' after applyTemplateVariables. Such a target is then classified and grouped as a normal (metric) query and sent downstream with an empty expression. If all targets interpolate to empty, runSplitQuery builds zero grouped requests and runSplitGroupedQueries() dereferences requests.filter(...)[0].partition after Math.max(...[]) , throwing a TypeError instead of completing with no data. The same regression is introduced in runShardSplitQuery(), which changed from interpolate-then-filter to filter-then-interpolate. Targets need to be filtered again after interpolation.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are only loaded for web requests

The only call to I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! is in ApplicationController#set_locale. Server-side translations also occur in Sidekiq jobs, mailers, rake tasks, and console/background processes, where this filter never runs. The lazy loader in translate_accelerator only loads config.locale, not the site-default or :en fallback locales, so in a job-only process those YAML files may never enter the backend store and a missing translation will return 'translation missing' instead of falling back. Fallback loading should be ensured from I18n.translate/load_locale or from the job/mailer locale setup, not only from the web controller.

Translation cache can retain missing or stale fallback results after locales load

The LRU cache key is only key + current locale + backend object_id, and load_locale/ensure_loaded! add translations without clearing @cache (only reload! clears it). If a key is first translated before its fallback locale has been loaded, the 'translation missing' string produced for that lookup is stored by getset and will keep being returned after the fallback file is loaded, until eviction or reload. The same staleness occurs when SiteSetting.default_locale changes, because FallbackLocaleList then points at a different fallback locale while the cache key is unchanged, so strings cached from the old fallback locale continue to be served. Loading a locale should invalidate the cache, or missing results and the effective fallback chain must be accounted for in caching.

Fallback lookup consults SiteSetting on every translation

I18n::Backend::Fallbacks invokes I18n.fallbacks[locale] for each backend translation, and the translate accelerator bypasses its cache for the common calls that pass interpolation, count, or locale options. This implementation therefore rebuilds the fallback array and calls the DB-backed SiteSetting.default_locale (with to_sym) on a per-translation hot path, and makes plain I18n.t depend on site-settings availability even in boot or isolated job contexts. The chain should be computed when the locale/site default is set, or memoized keyed by the current site/default locale with invalidation when that setting changes.

No tests cover the new fallback behavior

The PR adds FallbackLocaleList, fallback-backend inclusion, lazy fallback loading, and a controller hook, but adds no specs. There is no coverage proving the user-locale -> site-default -> :en order, that fallback translation files are loaded on demand (including pluralized/interpolated keys that bypass the accelerator cache), or that non-controller translation paths fall back correctly. Such tests are needed because the failure mode is silent: missing keys degrade to 'translation missing' strings rather than raising in production.

Public group members page now silently shows only the first 50 members

The public group/members template and GroupMembers route were not given any pagination controls or follow-up fetching, so members beyond the first 50 of a large group are unreachable in the public UI.

A request such as members.json?limit=-1 or offset=-1 can produce a database error/500, limit=0 returns a meta limit of 0 that breaks client page calculations, and a huge limit lets any user who can see a group serialize its entire membership in one request, defeating the new pagination and creating an expensive response for large automatic groups. The client sends alias_level in Group#asJSON and the group form shows the alias-level selector for unsaved groups, but Admin::GroupsController#create only assigns name and visible. The old PATCH branch that applied changes:{add,delete} has been removed, but Rails still routes PATCH to #update. Validation is not a one-time commit event: UsersController#create calls user.valid? and then user.save (which validates again), so one blocked signup attempt increments the counter at least twice, and any other code that merely calls valid?/save on a user with a changed email also records a 'match' even if the user is never persisted. The candidate adds the double-counting consequence, but it states that the predicate or validator should be side-effect free, which is the core concern in the golden comment.

A blocked address such as bad@spam.com can therefore be resubmitted as Bad@Spam.com or with surrounding whitespace and miss the block, while the case-insensitive portions of Discourse treat those as the same email. The unique database/model check is likewise case-sensitive, so differently-cased duplicates of a blocked address can coexist. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same flaw: BlockedEmail.should_block? does a case-sensitive email lookup, so a differently-cased address can get past the block. The candidate raises extra points (whitespace, uniqueness), but the core issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
match_count increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write

Two concurrent registration attempts matching the same blocked email can read the same count and both save count+1, losing an increment, and the full-record save can also overwrite concurrent changes to fields such as action_type. Use an atomic database increment (e.g. update_counters/increment_counter or a single UPDATE ... SET match_count = match_count + 1) for the statistics update.

Since User now relies on `validates :email, email: true` (app/models/user.rb:47) as its email validator, a direct API request with a malformed value such as 'not-an-email' passes server-side validation as long as it is present and unique, creating an account whose activation/welcome mail can never be delivered. The validator spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and calls validate_each directly on a fabricated user, while blocked_email_spec tests BlockedEmail in isolation. Nothing exercises the full path that a User with a real blocked email fails to save through `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, so a broken validator registration, autoload problem, or email_changed? condition would let blocked signups through while all new specs still pass. It also emits -ms-align-items, which is not the IE10 property. The mixin should translate flex-start/flex-end to start/end for the legacy properties. Current callers use center and baseline, which happen to be spelled the same in both syntaxes.

The mixin copies $val directly to -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group, but legacy ordinal groups are 1-based (initial value 1 and values below 1 are invalid) while flex order is 0-based (initial value 0). Consequently order(0) emits an invalid legacy declaration and the legacy translation does not faithfully represent the standard value; the legacy properties should use $val + 1.

The new method is named `include_website_name` without `?`, so it is never invoked: `website_name` is serialized for every user, with a nil value when the user has no website, instead of being omitted as intended.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses the untrusted-user field restrictions

`website_name` is added to the public attributes but not to the `untrusted_attributes` list (lines 105-111), which hides fields such as `website`, `location` and `bio_cooked` from anonymous viewers of TL0 users via scope.restrict_user_fields?. Because website_name is derived directly from the hidden website, an anonymous visitor can still learn a TL0/spam account's website host and, in the same-domain case, its full path, defeating the restriction that hides `website` itself.

The display text is built as `website_host + URI(website).path`, so for a website such as `http://example.com/blog?author=alice` or `http://example.com/#about` the serialized name becomes just `example.com/blog` or `example.com/`. The elsif branch treats two hosts as the same base domain only when they have the same number of labels and everything after the first label matches (e.g. www.example.com vs forum.example.com). The new specs cover only an unrelated domain, an exact host match, and a parent-domain website. They do not exercise the elsif sibling-subdomain branch in website_name (www.example.com vs forum.example.com, or the negative case where the remaining labels differ), nor the TL0-user-seen-as-anonymous context at the top of the file, so neither a regression in that branch nor website_name leaking for restricted users would be caught.

The URL is checked only for an http/https prefix, so a URL containing a single quote or markup can close the attribute or element and inject additional HTML. Because the resulting post uses raw_html cooking, that injected markup is stored and rendered without the normal cooking sanitization.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

poll_feed unconditionally calls i.content.scrub for every feed item. RSS items commonly provide only a description or summary and can therefore have nil content, raising NoMethodError. Because there is no per-item rescue, one such item aborts the entire hourly poll, prevents all remaining items from being imported, and will recur on every run until the feed changes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: calling i.content.scrub when content is nil, because RSS items often supply only a description, which raises NoMethodError and crashes the poll. The candidate adds detail about the impact.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Referer is embedded unescaped in a JavaScript string

The embed layout interpolates request.referer directly inside a single-quoted JavaScript string passed to parent.postMessage. A referer containing an apostrophe or crafted path can terminate the string and alter the script executed on the Discourse-origin embed page. The target origin should be derived and serialized safely on the server, for example by extracting the referer's origin and emitting it with proper JavaScript/JSON escaping.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same issue: request.referer is interpolated unescaped into JavaScript, which allows script injection (XSS). The candidate adds detail about the postMessage call and how to fix it, but the underlying bug is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
Imported feed HTML is stored and rendered without sanitization

TopicEmbed.import creates posts with cook_method raw_html for content supplied by Jobs::PollFeed, and Post#cook returns that raw content verbatim as cooked HTML. The PollFeed path does not pass the content through Readability or any HTML sanitizer, so script elements, event-handler attributes, javascript: URLs, and other active markup from an RSS/Atom item are persisted and later rendered to forum readers. This is a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability if any imported feed item contains malicious or compromised content.

Unknown embeds enqueue an unbounded retrieval job on every request

EmbedController#best enqueues Jobs::RetrieveTopic whenever no TopicEmbed exists, with no controller-side throttling or deduplication. The 60-second throttle is only checked after a job is dequeued, and the loading page automatically reloads, while non-browser clients can spoof the Referer check trivially. Repeated or malicious requests for a URL that can never be retrieved can therefore flood the Sidekiq queue indefinitely.

Remote import fetches arbitrary redirected URLs without timeouts or size limits

TopicEmbed.import_remote calls open(url).read with no timeout, response-size limit, or validation of the final URI after redirects. TopicRetriever validates only the initial embed_url host, so a page on the embeddable host can redirect the server-side request to another host, including internal services, and a slow or very large response can tie up a background worker or exhaust memory. A bounded HTTP fetch that revalidates redirect targets is needed.

Disqus import now depends on live remote pages and aborts on fetch failures

The Disqus importer replaces local topic creation with TopicEmbed.import_remote for each thread link. If a link is missing, stale, offline, or returns an HTTP error, open() raises and aborts the whole Thor import, leaving later threads unprocessed; if import_remote returns no post, that thread's Disqus comments are silently skipped. Previously the topic could be created from the export itself, so this change risks losing exported comments solely because the original site is unavailable.

Embed controller spec expects synchronous retrieval the controller no longer performs

The spec expects TopicRetriever.new and retrieve to be called when no embed exists, but EmbedController#best never references TopicRetriever; it enqueues Jobs::RetrieveTopic instead. Mocha will report the unmet TopicRetriever expectation, so this test fails and provides no valid coverage of the actual enqueue behavior. The spec should expect the retrieve_topic job enqueue with the user id and embed_url.

Protocol-relative URLs are incorrectly rewritten to the source host

absolutize_urls treats every href or src beginning with '/' as a path on the source host. Protocol-relative URLs such as //cdn.example.com/image.jpg therefore become http://source-host/cdn.example.com/image.jpg instead of retaining the CDN host, breaking external links and images in imported content; the same faulty transformation is applied to img src attributes below. Protocol-relative and ordinary relative URLs need distinct handling.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

Second downsize definition overrides the existing width/height API

Ruby does not support method overloading by arity. This new three-argument downsize definition replaces the width/height version defined immediately above it at lines 145-147. Existing callers using downsize(from, to, width, height) will now treat width as a complete dimensions string and height as opts, producing wrong geometry or a TypeError, while callers passing width, height, and opts will raise ArgumentError. The old signature must be retained compatibly or every existing caller updated.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem. The downsize method is defined a second time with a dimensions-string signature, which overrides the earlier width/height version. That makes the original unreachable and breaks existing callers that pass separate width and height arguments.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hard-coded 10 MB client limit ignores per-type site settings

validateUploadedFile receives a type and previously used the corresponding max_image_size_kb or max_attachment_size_kb setting. Replacing that lookup with a fixed 10 MB value means attachments larger than 10 MB are rejected even when the site allows them, while non-image attachments above a lower configured attachment limit pass the client check, are not downsized by the server, and then fail only after being uploaded. The same hard-coded value is repeated for the 413 error at line 246. The image pre-downsizing allowance should not replace attachment validation or disregard configured limits.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the hardcoded 10MB limit for ignoring the per-type max_*_size_kb site settings, and both note that the 413 handler has the same problem. They describe the same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
In-place downsizing ignores conversion failure and can destroy the upload

OptimizedImage.downsize returns false when conversion or optimization fails, but this call ignores the result and uses the same tempfile path as both input and output. A failed or partial ImageMagick/ImageOptim operation can therefore truncate or corrupt the only copy of the uploaded file, after which the loop retries the failed operation up to five times and line 72 proceeds with whatever remains. Downsizing should write to a separate file, check the result, and only replace the original after success.

No server-side size limit is enforced before expensive image conversion

The 10 MB limits added elsewhere are only in client-side JavaScript and in the URL-download branch. A direct multipart request can bypass JavaScript and submit a much larger image, causing this code to run as many as five full ImageMagick and ImageOptim passes before Upload.create_for performs its normal size validation. An authenticated user can consequently trigger very large CPU, memory, and disk consumption, including with a highly compressed image that expands greatly when decoded. The controller should enforce the intended maximum input size server-side before invoking downsizing.

Downsizing is applied unsafely to SVG and animated image originals

The condition accepts every filename considered an image and sends it through convert with the first-frame selector. This bypasses the SVG special case elsewhere in OptimizedImage, where SVG files are copied rather than converted, so an oversized vector can be rasterized, invalidated, or changed in format. Likewise, when animated thumbnails are disabled, an animated GIF original is reduced to its first frame rather than merely having a static thumbnail. SVG handling and preservation of animation for the stored original need separate treatment.

The pull request adds a percentage-based OptimizedImage.downsize form, a five-attempt controller loop, changed client limits, and changed download limits, but includes no spec or JavaScript test changes. There is therefore no coverage proving percentage geometry works, that the loop terminates at the configured byte limit, that conversion failure preserves or rejects the upload safely, or that animated and vector images retain their expected format.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

State-changing unsubscribe is performed by an unauthenticated-token GET request

Calendar update uses the caller's credentials instead of the booking organizer's

The handler explicitly permits non-organizers (team admins/owners and attendees), but then calls getUsersCredentials(ctx.user) and constructs EventManager from ctx.user. For those callers this does not contain the booking organizer's calendar credential/destination calendar, even though the booking query loaded booking.user with credentials. updateCalendarAttendees can therefore fail to update the organizer's external calendar, or attempt to use an unrelated credential of the caller, while the database attendees and emails claim the guests were added. The organizer's booking user/credentials should drive the calendar update.

Guests can be added to cancelled, rejected, pending, or past bookings

After loading the booking, the handler never checks booking.status or whether the event has ended before inserting attendees, updating the calendar, and sending emails. The new email templates generate ICS data with status CONFIRMED, so adding a guest to a cancelled booking can send a confirmed invitation and push attendees back toward the external calendar event, and adding guests to a past event sends meaningless invitations. The mutation, and ideally the UI action, should be restricted to appropriate upcoming confirmed bookings.

Guest list has no maximum size

guests is an unbounded array of emails. An authorized caller can submit thousands of addresses in one mutation, causing a large createMany, one translation load per attendee, a calendar update, and an email fan-out to every attendee. This enables resource exhaustion and use of the deployment as an invitation-email relay. Add a reasonable server-side max (and min) to the schema rather than relying on the dialog UI.

Invalid-email error state is not reset after success or dialog dismissal

isInvalidEmail is set when validation fails, but the mutation onSuccess only resets multiEmailValue and closes the dialog; it does not reset isInvalidEmail. Closing via the dialog's onOpenChange (for example the X/Escape path) also bypasses the Cancel button's reset. Reopening Add Guests after a corrected, successful submission can therefore show 'Emails must be unique and valid' above a fresh empty form. Reset the flag on success and whenever the dialog closes or its value changes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code comparison does not normalize case or whitespace

Generated codes are lowercase hex, but verification only strips '-' via replaceAll before indexOf; it does not trim whitespace or lowercase the input. A user who types the code in uppercase (as suggested by the XXXXX-XXXXX placeholder), or pastes it with surrounding whitespace, is rejected with IncorrectBackupCode even though they entered the correct code. The same un-normalized comparison exists in the disable-2FA endpoint, so normalization should be applied consistently in both places.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem: backup code validation with indexOf is case-sensitive, so uppercase input fails. The candidate also raises whitespace, but the core issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code consumption is not atomic, allowing concurrent reuse

The code reads the encrypted backup-code list, marks the matched entry null, and writes the whole list back without a transaction, conditional update, or lock. Two concurrent login requests using the same backup code can both read the list before either writes, both find the code, and both authenticate, violating the documented exactly-once property of backup codes. Consumption needs to be made atomic so only one request can claim a code.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same race condition. Backup codes are read, mutated in memory, and written back non-atomically, so concurrent logins can reuse a single backup code.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
resetState leaves backup codes, secret, and download URL in memory

resetState only clears the password, error, and step; it never clears backupCodes, dataUri, secret, or backupCodesUrl, and never revokes the Blob object URL. The modal component stays mounted after Close/Cancel, so the plaintext backup codes and a working download URL for them remain live in the page for as long as it is open, contrary to the expectation that closing the backup-code screen discards them. Clear those states and call URL.revokeObjectURL in resetState.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say the backup codes Blob object URL is never revoked. The golden comment frames this as a memory leak on unmount. The candidate frames it as a security and state-clearing problem in resetState on close, but it explicitly calls for URL.revokeObjectURL. The location and framing differ slightly, yet the underlying issue of the unrevoked object URL is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code can bypass password verification

Password verification is skipped whenever credentials.totpCode is non-empty, while the new branch at line 131 authenticates whenever credentials.backupCode is valid and ignores the TOTP code. An attacker can therefore send a dummy totpCode together with a valid backup code and no correct password and be logged in. A leaked or guessed backup code thus becomes a single-factor credential instead of a replacement second factor; password verification must also run when backupCode is supplied (or whenever the account has a password and this is not the password-less external-TOTP flow).

Users with pre-existing 2FA can never obtain backup codes

Users who enabled 2FA before this feature have backupCodes = null. The setup endpoint rejects anyone with twoFactorEnabled already true, and this PR adds no endpoint or settings UI to generate backup codes for an already-enabled account. Such users who click 'Lost access' only get MissingBackupCodes and a message telling them to generate codes in settings, which is impossible without disabling and re-enabling 2FA (and the message does not say that), leaving the recovery path a dead end for all existing 2FA users.

No test exercises logging in or disabling with a backup code

The added e2e coverage only checks that the download/copy/close buttons work after enabling 2FA; as the TODO on this line admits, nothing tests the actual new authentication paths: login with a backup code, disabling 2FA with a backup code, rejection of a wrong code, or rejection when reusing an already-consumed code. These are the security-critical behaviors of the feature (especially single-use invalidation in next-auth-options.ts), and the PR description's own checklist confirms no such tests were added, so a regression in them would ship undetected.

Password visibility toggle is removed from keyboard navigation globally

Adding tabIndex={-1} to the show/hide-password button in the shared PasswordField makes the toggle unreachable by keyboard for every form in the app, not just the 2FA modals this PR touches. Keyboard and assistive-technology users can no longer reveal a typed password to check it. This unrelated global accessibility regression should be reverted or scoped to the specific field that motivated it.

Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google updateEvent fallback cannot find the destination calendar

In GoogleCalendarService.updateEvent, when externalCalendarId is falsy the fallback searches for `cal.externalId === externalCalendarId`, comparing calendar IDs to the same falsy value that triggered the fallback, so selectedCalendar is always undefined. calendar.events.update is then called with calendarId undefined and fails, whereas the previous code used the event's destination calendar externalId.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same faulty lookup in Google updateEvent, `cal.externalId === externalCalendarId`, which compares the calendar ID against the very value used to select the fallback, so it can never find the intended calendar. The golden comment frames the trigger condition a little differently (when the ID is provided) than the candidate (when it is falsy), but the underlying self-referential logic bug is identical.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Office365 createEvent ignores credential-specific destination calendar

Office365CalendarService.createEvent always uses the first entry of event.destinationCalendar as mainHostDestinationCalendar and does not accept or use the credentialId now passed by CalendarManager. For collective events, EventManager calls this once per host credential, so a second Office365 host's event is attempted against the main host's calendar externalId with the second host's token, causing failures or an event targeted at the wrong calendar.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate points out that Office365 createEvent does not accept the credentialId parameter, which is the same thing the golden comment flags as breaking the interface signature. The candidate frames it mainly as a runtime calendar-selection bug, but the underlying code issue is identical: the implementation is missing the credentialId parameter.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateAllCalendarEvents can reuse the previous reference's credential

In EventManager.updateAllCalendarEvents, `credential` is declared outside the loop over calendar references. If a later reference's credential is not in calendarCredentials and the DB lookup does not produce a credential, the variable still holds the previous iteration's credential, and updateEvent is pushed with that wrong credential. That can update the previous host's calendar again and leave the intended host's event unchanged.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same spot: the credential lookup fails for a reference with a credentialId, and the result is still passed to updateEvent. The golden comment says the credential is undefined, which causes a crash. The candidate says a stale credential from the previous loop iteration is reused, which updates the wrong calendar. The underlying issue is the same missing handling when the credential is not found, though the described consequence differs.

false_positives.candidate:
Google Meet fallback crashes when destinationCalendar is empty or absent

In EventManager.create, evt.destinationCalendar is destructured with `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []`, which yields undefined when the array is empty or missing, but the next condition dereferences `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. For a Google Meet booking with no destination calendar this throws a TypeError instead of falling back to Cal Video, breaking booking creation.

Google createEvent uses main host organizer email for every host calendar

In GoogleCalendarService.createEvent, selectedCalendar is correctly chosen by matching credentialId, but the payload organizer email still comes from mainHostDestinationCalendar, the first destinationCalendar entry, for every credential. When EventManager creates the event on a second collective host's Google calendar, that event is created with the main host's calendar/externalId as organizer email, which does not match the authenticated host and can produce a wrong organizer or rejected/misattributed event.

Lark createEvent always targets the first destination calendar

LarkCalendarService.createEvent derives calendarId only from the first destinationCalendar entry and does not use the credentialId supplied for the new multi-destination flow. When EventManager loops over collective hosts and invokes Lark for another host, it will reuse the main host's Lark calendar ID with that host's credentials, so creation fails or targets the wrong calendar instead of that host's destination calendar.

CalDAV createEvent can silently create no event for non-main hosts

BaseCalendarService.createEvent filters the credential's calendars to those matching mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId, always the first destination calendar. For a second collective host using CalDAV, that externalId is a calendar URL from the main host's server and normally matches none of this host's calendars; the Promise.all then resolves over an empty list and the method returns a generated uid as success even though no calendar object was created, leaving a booking reference pointing to a nonexistent event.

Video booking references lose their credentialId on creation

In EventManager.create, referencesToCreate now sets `credentialId: isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined`, so non-calendar results such as video meetings always get credentialId undefined. Previously video results preserved result.credentialId. Later cancellation and update flows look up the video credential by booking reference credentialId, so losing it can prevent the video meeting from being updated or deleted.

updateLocation creates calendar references without externalCalendarId or credentialId

In EventManager.updateLocation, references are built from result.externalId and result.credentialId, but CalendarManager.updateEvent does not return externalId or credentialId in its EventResult. Calendar references created after a location change therefore lose both identifiers, weakening later update/cancel operations that rely on reference.credentialId and reference.externalCalendarId to target the correct calendar.

Recurring collective cancellation repeatedly deletes only the first calendar reference

In handleCancelBooking's recurring/allRemainingBookings path, the code now loops over every calendar reference of the booking, but inside that loop it again iterates credentials and for each updated booking selects only `updBooking.references.find(ref => ref.type.includes('_calendar'))`, the first calendar reference. With multiple collective hosts this deletes the first host's recurring events repeatedly and never deletes the other hosts' calendar events, leaving orphaned events after cancellation.

Collective team destination calendars are dropped when organizer has none

In handleNewBooking, evt.destinationCalendar is set to null when neither eventType.destinationCalendar nor organizerUser.destinationCalendar exists, and the collective handling later does `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`. If only non-organizer collective hosts have destination calendars, teamDestinationCalendars is collected but never added because the optional-chained push is a no-op on null, so those hosts receive no calendar events.

Confirming a collective booking only creates the organizer's calendar event

confirmHandler builds evt.destinationCalendar from only booking.destinationCalendar or the confirming user's destinationCalendar, converted to a one-element array. For collective bookings that require confirmation, calendar events are created at confirmation time via this evt, so the other fixed hosts' destination calendars are never passed to EventManager and those hosts do not get calendar events when the booking is confirmed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.
The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach leaves calendar/video deletions unawaited

bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...) discards the callback promises. Now that getCalendar must be awaited, deleteEvent/deleteMeeting are not even invoked before the function sends the reschedule email and returns true; in a short-lived/serverless invocation they can be dropped, and any rejection becomes an unhandled rejection rather than being caught by the surrounding try/catch, which only catches synchronous errors. Replace forEach with await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...)) so deletions complete and failures are logged.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same issue. forEach with an async callback leaves the calendar/video deletions unawaited. Rejections become unhandled and escape the try/catch. Both recommend Promise.all with map as the fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are executed eagerly instead of lazily

Every value in the appStore object is created by immediately calling import(), so merely importing appStore starts loading all 29 app modules, including apps unrelated to the current request. This defeats the intended lazy/code-split loading, adds startup and module-evaluation cost to every consumer of getCalendar, videoClient, and payment code, and creates rejected promises for unused apps that may surface as unhandled rejections if a module fails to load. Store loader functions such as () => import('./applecalendar') and invoke them at call sites, or provide an async getter.

requestReschedule does not await async calendar/video deletions

bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...) discards the callback promises. After this change the callbacks suspend at await getCalendar, while the mutation immediately proceeds to send the reschedule email and webhooks and can finish before the old calendar/video events are deleted, leaving orphan events that keep the old time busy; failures are also unhandled rejections. Use await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...)) before sending the email/returning.

Recurring-booking calendar deletions race past apiDeletes collection

In the allRemainingBookings recurring branch, credentials are processed with .forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(...) }). Those callbacks suspend at the await, so when line 652 later evaluates Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)), concat snapshots an apiDeletes array that does not yet contain the calendar deletions. The handler can therefore delete attendees/booking references and return while recurring calendar events are still present or never deleted, and deletion errors are unhandled. Replace the async forEach with a for...of loop or await Promise.all(...map(...)) that populates apiDeletes before it is awaited.
